CDTFA, Tax Guide for Membership Fees (https://cdtfa.ca.gov/industry/membership-fees/): 'Membership fees that grant access to health club facilities, such as a gym or a massage facility, are generally not taxable even if the operator sells consumables, fitness and wellness merchandise, or other miscellaneous items on the premises.' Chains still print 'taxes may apply' as boilerplate.

gym_tax_notes_by_region.treatment: Standard rate 20%. Commercial, profit-distributing gyms and health clubs (PureGym, The Gym Group, Third Space, Virgin Active) charge VAT at 20% on memberships. Supplies of sport and physical education by 'eligible bodies' (non-profit, non-distribution clause, profits reinvested in facilities, not under commercial influence), including many leisure trusts operating council centres, are VAT-exempt (VAT Notice 701/45). Consumer prices are shown VAT-inclusive as required by UK price-marking law, so the published figure is what the member pays either way.

Gymnasium (commercial) membership fees — right of admission including use of facilities — are liable at the second reduced rate, 9% (current rates from 1 Jan 2026: standard 23%, reduced 13.5%, second reduced 9%; sporting-facilities item in the 9% band from 1 May 2022 to 31 Dec 2030 per Revenue). Separately charged aerobic/keep-fit classes are at the reduced rate, 13.5%. Facilities provided by non-profit organisations are outside this charge (exempt). Irish consumer prices are quoted VAT-inclusive.
Current Irish VAT rates from 1 January 2026: standard 23%, reduced 13.5%, second reduced 9%.

Gym and fitness memberships are taxable supplies under the GST/HST; Ontario HST rate is 13% (5% federal + 8% provincial). All Toronto chains read here (Fit4Less, Planet Fitness, YMCA GTA, City of Toronto) quote prices before tax.
GST 5% applies to gym memberships (BC is not an HST province). YWCA page: 'All memberships and services are subject to GST'; Fitness World and City of Vancouver quote prices before tax.

PST (7%) does not apply to memberships: 'No, PST does not apply to memberships, event admissions, or tickets and passes for sporting or music events, as long as no taxable goods (e.g. a t-shirt) are provided with the membership or admission.' So a Vancouver gym membership carries 5% GST only.
Gym memberships are independent services taxed at the general 16% IVA rate (not among art. 15 exemptions). CDMX is not in the northern/southern border 8% stimulus zone.

equipment_vs_bodyweight.claim: Low-load bench press and push-up produce similar hypertrophy and strength gain.
equipment_vs_bodyweight.finding: 18 untrained college men, 3 sets to failure at ~40% 1RM, twice weekly for 8 weeks. Pectoralis major thickness +19.4% (bench) vs +18.3% (push-up); triceps +10.3% vs +9.5%; 1RM +8.3% vs +5.1%; no significant between-group difference. Authors: push-up at a load similar to 40% 1RM bench press is 'comparably effective for muscle hypertrophy and strength gain'. Limitation noted for highly trained subjects.
equipment_vs_bodyweight.source: Kikuchi, N. and Nakazato, K. (2017), Journal of Exercise Science & Fitness 15(1): 37-42

equipment_vs_bodyweight.claim: Bench press and elastic-band push-up at matched muscle activity give similar strength gains.
equipment_vs_bodyweight.finding: 5-week training at 6RM: bench press group and elastic-band push-up group both improved 1RM and 6RM significantly with similar gains (changes ranging 13.65 to 22.21); control unchanged. Conclusion: when EMG levels are comparable the exercises give similar strength gains.
equipment_vs_bodyweight.source: Calatayud, J. et al. (2015), Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 29(1): 246-253

training_effect.conclusion: No published MET or training-effect penalty specific to 'bodyweight at home' versus 'equipment at a gym' was found. In the 2024 Adult Compendium the energy cost is set by effort, not by venue or equipment: vigorous weight lifting 6.0 vs vigorous calisthenics 7.5 and high-intensity bodyweight resistance 6.5; multi-exercise weight training 3.5 vs moderate calisthenics 3.8 and general bodyweight resistance 3.0; 'home exercise, general' is 3.8. Training studies show matched-effort bodyweight work (push-ups, banded push-ups) gives hypertrophy and strength gains statistically similar to bench press in untrained or short-term subjects. The one defensible difference is progression: bodyweight load is capped by body mass unless variations or bands are added, and Kikuchi and Nakazato flag that their result may not hold for highly trained people; no published figure quantifies that cap, so its size is null.
